title: The Big Law Pyramid Is Turning Into a Cylinder
author: Bryson Malcolm

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI is weakening junior-heavy staffing and extends it with a concrete successor model: a more cylindrical, top-heavy structure sustained by lateral hiring of already-trained lawyers. It also identifies profit-per-partner incentives and predicts that training reform will lag, although its causal claims rely mainly on examples and forecasts rather than profession-wide evidence.
qs: Talent that used to be stockpiled at the entry level is now picked off laterally, through recruiters, at exactly the seniority the firm needs.
For the next five to ten years, expect Big Law hiring to stay top-heavy.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will restructure production and associate leverage rather than eliminate lawyers, and materially extends the cluster by identifying PPP incentives for reducing junior headcount, forecasting a five-to-ten-year top-heavy hiring market, and proposing compressed, redesigned training for higher-level work.
qs: Reducing headcount and leverage juices profits per equity partner, and PPP is how the market scores a firm's success.

## Where this goes  At some point firms will adjust the training model so that entry-level attorneys do the high-level, thought-intensive work that AI cannot, and the economics of junior talent will make sense again.

kp.k: NALP trends indicate rapidly changing law-firm leverage
kp.d: Malcolm reports that recent NALP data shows firms making fewer equity partners while expanding senior non-equity roles. He defines leverage here as the ratio of equity partners to all other attorneys, but the article provides no underlying figures, sample details, or data period.
qs: The latest NALP data shows that shape changing, and the consequences will land on law students first.
The headline is that leverage is changing fast.
Firms are making fewer equity partners, which most people inside the industry already sensed. And they are growing the ranks of senior attorneys: counsel, non-equity partners, and senior associates.

kp.k: Hiring is shifting away from junior and mid-level lawyers
kp.d: The author characterises current hiring as concentrated among experienced lawyers rather than entry-level, junior, or mid-level associates. In his account, stagnant or declining entry classes are changing the traditional pyramid into a more cylindrical staffing structure.
qs: The hiring is happening at the top. It is no longer happening at the entry level, the junior level, or the mid-level.
What the data points to now is a cylinder. Firms are stopping the overhire at the base.
Summer classes have been shrinking steadily across the industry, and entry-level classes are stagnant or shrinking at many firms.

kp.k: Megafirms remain an exception to entry-level contraction
kp.d: Malcolm says a small group of very large firms can still absorb large summer and entry classes. He claims that contraction is instead concentrated in the tier below, naming Gibson Dunn and Cooley as firms that have reduced summer classes, without supplying class-size figures or dates.
qs: The exception is the handful of megafirms still growing, the Lathams, Kirklands, and Simpson Thachers of the world.
Those firms can afford big summer and entry classes because they run a machine large enough to absorb them.
The shrinking is concentrated in the tier just below: Gibson Dunn has reduced its summer class, Cooley has reduced its summer class, and many other firms are quietly doing the same.

kp.k: AI is asserted to substitute for junior-level work
kp.d: The article attributes entry-level contraction partly to AI, asserting that AI can perform much of a first-year attorney's work but not yet senior-attorney or partner work. This is presented as the author's explanation of the structural shift, without supporting task studies, performance measures, or adoption data.
qs: AI can already do much of the work of an entry-level attorney.
It cannot yet do the work of a senior attorney or a partner.
So firms are shrinking the bottom of the pyramid and buying experience on the lateral market when they need it.

kp.k: Lateral recruitment replaces internal junior-talent stockpiling
kp.d: Malcolm argues that firms below the largest megafirms increasingly expect to recruit experienced associates trained elsewhere. Under this proposed flow, megafirms retain large entry classes and high attrition, while other strong firms reduce summer hiring and fill later needs through lateral recruitment.
qs: Talent that used to be stockpiled at the entry level is now picked off laterally, through recruiters, at exactly the seniority the firm needs.
The behemoth firms keep their big entry classes, and their attrition stays high.
Those firms know the downflow is coming, so they trim their own summer classes and rely on lateral hiring to fill the gaps with attorneys someone else already trained.

kp.k: Lower leverage is linked to higher partner profits
kp.d: The author identifies a financial incentive alongside AI-enabled task substitution: reducing junior headcount and leverage can increase profits per equity partner, the metric he says the market uses to judge firm success. The article states this mechanism rather than quantifying its effect.
qs: There is a financial motive layered on top.
Reducing headcount and leverage juices profits per equity partner, and PPP is how the market scores a firm's success.
Fewer bodies at the bottom makes the top line look stronger, and firm leadership knows it.

kp.k: Classes of 2027 and 2028 face tighter recruitment
kp.d: Malcolm predicts that students entering firms over the next few years, particularly the JD classes of 2027 and 2028, will encounter greater competition. He agrees with NALP's reported view that the effect will not be fatal for most top-school students, but expects candidates to move down the firm-prestige hierarchy.
qs: The students entering firms over the next few years will feel the crunch first.
NALP does not project it as fatal, and I agree.
Most students at top schools will still land excellent Big Law jobs.
The effect is a slow notch down the prestige ladder.

kp.k: Pay may persist while prestige outcomes deteriorate
kp.d: The author predicts that lockstep Big Law salaries will initially obscure changes in graduate outcomes: students may receive similar pay at less prestigious firms, while the career consequences of that prestige difference accumulate over time.
qs: Compensation will look identical, because Big Law pays lockstep salaries on the same scale at nearly every firm.
The difference shows up in prestige: instead of Gibson Dunn, maybe you land at McDermott.
As an associate your paycheck is the same. Over a career, the gap compounds.

kp.k: Lower-ranked law schools face the greatest squeeze
kp.d: Malcolm expects displacement down the recruitment hierarchy: as top-school students accept positions at firms below their previous targets, students from lower-ranked schools will face the strongest pressure. This is a prospective market claim rather than a documented outcome in the article.
qs: And because the top students slide down a notch in the recruitment funnel, students at lower-ranked schools get squeezed hardest.
The seamless pipeline that top-school students have enjoyed for a generation is going to have more friction at every level.

kp.k: Training redesign could restore junior-lawyer economics
kp.d: The author argues that entry-level hiring could recover if firms redesign training so juniors undertake thought-intensive work beyond AI's capabilities. He nevertheless predicts slow progress because he considers Big Law inefficient at training and expects rebuilding its training systems to take years.
qs: At some point firms will adjust the training model so that entry-level attorneys do the high-level, thought-intensive work that AI cannot, and the economics of junior talent will make sense again.
I would not hold my breath.
Big Law has never been good at training talent efficiently, and rebuilding that machinery will take years.

kp.k: Experience differences are attributed to training repetitions
kp.d: Malcolm states his personal view that first- and third-year associates do not have a fundamental capability gap; instead, third-years have accumulated more training repetitions. He suggests that compressing those repetitions could eventually permit broader junior recruitment.
qs: Fundamentally, I do not believe there is a real capability gap between a first-year and a third-year associate.
The brain has the same horsepower. What the third-year has is training reps.
Once firms figure out how to compress those reps, the recruiting model may loosen up again.

kp.k: Top-heavy hiring is predicted for five to ten years
kp.d: The article concludes with a specific forecast that Big Law hiring will remain weighted toward experienced lawyers for the next five to ten years, conditional on firms not yet having developed more efficient ways to train junior lawyers.
qs: For the next five to ten years, expect Big Law hiring to stay top-heavy.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Malcolm argues that AI's ability to perform junior work is helping turn Big Law's staffing pyramid into a cylinder, with smaller entry cohorts and greater reliance on experienced lateral hires.
pts.d: Bryson Malcolm claims that AI can already perform much entry-level attorney work, but not senior attorney or partner work. He links this distinction to firms reducing junior recruitment and acquiring already-trained lawyers at the seniority needed. He describes fewer equity promotions alongside growth in counsel, non-equity partners and senior associates. In his account, megafirms continue training large entry cohorts, while firms a tier below recruit departing associates rather than train as many themselves. He also identifies a separate financial incentive: reducing headcount and leverage to increase profits per equity partner.

pts.k: Malcolm predicts tougher graduate recruitment and top-heavy hiring for five to ten years, with potential recovery if firms redesign junior training.
pts.d: He predicts that smaller entry cohorts will push students down the firm-prestige ladder, with the greatest squeeze on lower-ranked law schools. He expects most top-school students still to obtain strong Big Law jobs at comparable lockstep salaries, but argues that differences in firm prestige compound over a career. Longer term, he anticipates firms training juniors for thought-intensive work AI cannot perform, restoring junior hiring economics. His proposed mechanism is compressing training repetitions: he presents the first-year/third-year difference as training rather than underlying capability.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The staffing account invokes NALP hiring trends and named firm examples; the AI capability claim, causal explanation and longer-term forecasts are Malcolm's assertions rather than presented benchmark findings.
pts.d: Malcolm cites recent NALP data for changing staffing patterns, fewer equity partners and growth in senior ranks, but supplies no numerical results, reporting period or specific study title. He names Gibson Dunn and Cooley as reducing summer classes, and Latham, Kirkland and Simpson Thacher as exceptions still supporting large cohorts. No AI task benchmarks, adoption measurements or firm testimony are supplied to establish AI's claimed capabilities or its causal role in these staffing changes. His perspective is that of Mosaic Search Partners' founder and CEO; the article does not present a systematic recruiter dataset. The training-capability argument is explicitly framed as his belief. He also attributes a non-catastrophic outlook to NALP and endorses it.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The shift is described as underway in June 2026, with near-term consequences for the JD classes of 2027 and 2028 and top-heavy hiring lasting another five to ten years.
pts.d: AI's junior-work capability and inability to do senior or partner work are qualified as current conditions, not permanent limits. Malcolm identifies the next few years as the immediate recruitment crunch. His forecast is not uniform across firms: a handful of growing megafirms retain large classes because they can absorb them, while contraction is concentrated a tier below. A subsequent loosening of recruitment depends on firms compressing training repetitions and preparing juniors for higher-level work; he expects this rebuilding to take years and offers no definite recovery date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects concern Big Law students and juniors, experienced lateral candidates, recruiting firms and equity partners, with unequal exposure across law-school and firm tiers.
pts.d: Students face fewer entry opportunities, particularly those at lower-ranked schools as higher-ranked students move down the recruitment funnel. Junior and mid-level lawyers are described as outside the main hiring growth, while senior associates, counsel and non-equity partners gain importance in firms' staffing strategies. Large growing firms remain training sources; firms a tier below rely more heavily on their departing associates. Recruiters facilitate targeted lateral acquisition. Equity partners benefit from the claimed profit incentive behind smaller headcounts. The article does not make concrete predictions about client outcomes, access to justice or legal-service quality.
